newsitem.title: UK: Bomb fans fears of N.Irish violence upsurge.
newsitem.headline: Bomb fans fears of N.Irish violence upsurge.

text.p: A Roman Catholic republican was wounded by a car bomb in Belfast on Sunday, heightening fears that Northern Ireland might be edging towards a new flare-up of sectarian violence.
Police said that four hours after the explosion in the heart of a strongly Catholic neighbourhood no group had claimed responsibility. "We don't know who is responsible yet," a spokesman said.
Politicians said they thought Protestant militants loyal to Britain were responsible and feared a highly praised, two-year ceasefire by Loyalist guerrillas could be over.
The 25-year-old victim, Eddie Copeland, a leading Irish republican in the Ardoyne district of north Belfast, sustained leg injuries which were not life threatening, police said.
A police source said the device, which exploded beneath the driver's seat, appeared to be a booby-trap.
It exploded when Copeland, who was wounded by a British soldier who went berserk in Ardoyne three years, got into the car after visiting his mother's house.
A neighbour said he rushed to Copeland's aid. "He was lying in the car. His leg was in a bad way. He was in agony. I put a towel to bind his leg to staunch the bleeding," he said.
"The windows were blown out in houses next door," Bobby Lavery, a local councillor for Sinn Fein, told reporters as British troops and armed police stood guard by the damaged car.
Sinn Fein is the political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which wants to oust Britain from Northern Ireland.
Security sources said that much of Copeland's car had been left intact and they hoped to find evidence from the make-up of the bomb that would enable them to identify which group made it.

"Loyalist" guerrillas have operated a truce for two years but at the weekend political sources close to them said they were coming under new pressure after IRA gunmen wounded a policeman at a Belfast children's hospital on Friday.
They warned that the Protestant militias might retaliate against Catholic nationalists.
"I think it is potentially the beginning of a spiral," said David Ervine, a leader of the Progressive Unionist Party, the political arm of the outlawed Loyalist Ulster Volunteer Force.
Ken Maginnis, security spokesman for the pro-British Ulster Unionst Party, which speaks for majority Protestants, denounced the bombing as "perhaps predictable retaliation".
Andrew Hunter, a member of Parliament for the ruling Conservative Party who specialises in Northern Ireland political affairs, also pointed the figure at loyalists.
"It has all the hallmarks of Loyalist retaliation following a crescendo of IRA provocation over the last fortnight or so," he said, speaking in London.

The hospital attack was the first shooting by the IRA since the guerrilla organisation ended a 17-month truce last February. It came hours after police warned that the republican guerrillas might strike at any time.
IRA bombers, fighting to establish an all-Ireland state, killed a soldier in car bomb attack at a British garrison south of Belfast in October.
They have bombed several targets chiefly in mainland Britain since February. Britain and Ireland says the IRA must abandon violence before Sinn Fein can join talks on the region's future.
